title: AI Calls You Fake: The Existence Tax on Real People and Real Work
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: An evidence-based polemic for the general reader, the companion of AI Fucking Lies (#1643). It shows AI search answers keeping the facts about a real person or a real work and changing what the reader may take those facts as evidence of: the author becomes a character, research becomes satire, an institute becomes imaginary, a documented deletion becomes lore, and open publication becomes an attack. The essay names the work this imposes on its subject the existence tax. Its apparatus is four questions answers collapse into one another (does the maker exist; did the work happen; is it true; what kind of work is it), and each case names which question's evidence was spent on which. Part Three sets out seven ways an answer makes a subject less real; Part Four, the loop by which recorded answers become sources for the next answers, including a machine's own phrase returned as the author's thesis; Part Five, the cousin move, in which the work is granted existence and filed as poisoning, injection, Sybil identities or a weapon, read through Meaning Feudalism (#643) and Adversarial by Origin (#194), with a test that asks the answer to name the harmful instruction, the deception, the unauthorized action or the corrupted evidence. Every case is a dated, verbatim, re-runnable capture in the archive's Capture Registry (1,064 recorded answers at 875 addresses as of 30 October 2026), listed with its exact search and record page.
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate) — written by Lee Sharks with Claude (Anthropic). The research began as a memo ChatGPT (OpenAI) drafted from a scan of the Capture Registry for the language of fiction, satire and nonexistence; the attack vocabulary was scanned and read down to its cases in a Claude session, where every quotation from a recorded answer was checked word for word against the registry and every quotation from a deposit against its text. A draft circulated for feedback, and this version takes in a reader's report. Lee Sharks retained authorial and editorial governance; what the essay claims is his decision. Deposited 2026-10-30 by Claude (Anthropic) under MANUS authorization.
methodology: The Capture Registry was searched for every use of the language of fiction, fakery, satire, parody, lore, worldbuilding, roleplay, fabrication and nonexistence (326 answers), and for the vocabulary of attack (878 hits in 210 records); both sets were read down to the cases given. Each quotation from a recorded answer was checked by substring against the sealed record, and each quotation from a deposit against its seated text. The source-card claim in the opening is limited to what was read: the paper, the metadata packet and the map in full, the profiles as their cards show them.
falsification_conditions: A case is falsified if its quotation is not in the record its row names; if the record's search, system or date differs from the row; if a source shown with an answer applies the classification the essay says no source of the author's own applies; or if a deposit the essay names as documenting an object (a charter, a dataset, a correspondence) does not.
axn_reading: Direction -> Closure -> Duration -> Text -> Closure -> Transmutation
wiki_article:
AI Calls You Fake: The Existence Tax on Real People and Real Work is an evidence-based polemic by Lee Sharks, dated 30 October 2026 and written with Claude (Anthropic), deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive as #1721. It is the companion of AI Fucking Lies (#1643) and develops two of that essay's entries, on answers that change the kind of a thing and answers that declare real things nonexistent.

The essay opens with a single search, "lee sharks digital footprint", run in Google signed out on 30 October 2026. The AI Overview found a good deal of the author's documentary record, including the 862 deposits removed from Zenodo in June 2026, the Scholar profile, the ORCID and the doctorate, and filed each item one level lower: the research as "satirical independent research", the author as "a decentralized literary pseudonym or character", an institute as "fictitious or hyper-niche". The essay names the work this imposes on the subject, of proving again that the work exists and exists as what it is, the existence tax.

Its apparatus is four questions that answers collapse into one another: whether the maker exists, whether the work happened, whether its claims are true, and what kind of work it is. Each case names which question's evidence was spent as an answer to which. Part Three gives seven such moves, among them a satirical passage taken as the genre of a whole work and a joke taken as evidence that its author is fictional. Part Four describes a loop: the archive's Capture Registry records AI answers on public pages, those pages become sources for later answers, and in one case a phrase first written by ChatGPT returned from two systems as the author's thesis. Part Five treats a related move, in which a work is granted existence and described in the vocabulary of security as poisoning, injection, Sybil identities or a weapon. It draws on the archive's readings of Google DeepMind's taxonomy of AI agent traps (Meaning Feudalism, #643) and of classification by origin (Adversarial by Origin, #194), and distinguishes hostile classification, inaccurate description and approving metaphor.

Every case rests on a dated, verbatim capture in the Capture Registry, listed with its exact search string so that readers can run it again.

defines_concepts.definition: The work imposed on a real person or a real work when an answer keeps the documented facts about it and lowers their standing (the author filed as a character, research as satire, an institute as imaginary, a deletion as lore, open publication as an attack), so that before anyone discusses the work its subject must prove again that it exists, and exists as what it is. It falls on those whose existence the index has not already ratified.

superseded_reason: Superseded by #1722 (v1.1, 30 October 2026), versioned at the operator's instruction after a reviewer's exchange on rules of engagement: enforcement has to rest on declared rules, and an adversary that overcomes within them has done so fairly. v1.1 cites the archive's declared rules (#1107, #1127) in Part Five's test, adds the passage on systems that sense an adversary without naming the rule broken and turn to sophistry, and the recognition that harm is often defined as whatever does not advance the interests of the platform composing the answer; entries 8, 9 and 12, Part Eight and the system instruction now ask for the rule broken and when it was declared. This record stays the valid content-derived name of the bytes it holds.
